issues.body: `stub_with_timeout` creates `sparq-oracle-stub-<pid>-<counter>.py` directly in the shared temp directory using `fs::write`, then executes that path with Python. The symlink regression test similarly creates predictable `sparq-oracle-victim-<pid>.txt` with `fs::write`. Another local user can pre-create either path as a symlink: the test runner will overwrite the link target, and the stub case can additionally execute attacker-controlled contents if the target is replaced between writing and spawning. Thus the production fix moves the prior vulnerability out of `Scratch` but leaves the same unsafe pattern in code run by `cargo test`.
issues.fix_hint: Create stub scripts and the victim inside private `tempfile::TempDir` instances (owner-only), or use `NamedTempFile`/atomic `create_new(true)` handles and execute via the securely created path. Avoid all PID/counter-derived files directly under the shared temp directory. Keep the planted paths predictable only as inert symlinks used to challenge production `Scratch`; place the victim and executable stub in private temporary directories.
issues.title: Test helpers retain predictable shared-temp symlink vulnerabilities

verdict.summary: The production scratch-path vulnerability from round 2 is fixed with an owner-only tempfile directory, and the new test exercises that production invariant. However, the test infrastructure itself introduces the same predictable-path/symlink class in `stub_with_timeout` and in the symlink regression test's victim setup. A local user can pre-create those PID/counter-derived paths: the test then follows the link with `fs::write`, potentially overwriting a file writable by the test runner; for the Python stub path, this can also substitute attacker-controlled code that the test immediately executes. Because a new major security finding remains, changes are requested and progress is regressing.
